**Q:** Does it mean that I can always use gradient descent to find the lowest error, or find the parameter to make sure that my loss is zero, is perfect?

At this point in time, almost everything is done in deep learning. Uber uses deep learning to predict ETA, and part of my job is to also build models to predict very accurate ETA. You'll see things like your medical devices, image segmentation, image classification, we will see on Thursday. Your large language model is all based on deep learning. From a very interesting standpoint, a very interesting backstory, neural networks was created because we want to follow the structure of the human brain. You will see that everything can be expressed in math later on. The idea here is that you think of each of these individual layers as neurons. What we want to do is we just want to pass, and we want to architect. Think of neural networks like Lego blocks. The expressive power comes from the fact that you can define the different Lego blocks. If you think about Lego blocks on its own, each Lego block is useless. It's very small, just a square. But when you put all the Lego blocks together, you have something very impressive to express something. Same thing as the neural network. You realize today that what we are trying to learn are very basic fundamental math using matrix algebra, using linear algebra. Each of these components, you can think of them as Lego blocks, that now you can build. You have the ability to build all kinds of complex neural networks, which could allow you to have some kind of expressive power. But then, what makes this superpower also makes it challenging to build. Because now you are trying to build a Lego block, unlike the previous machine learning algorithm, where the algorithm is already defined. Now, you not just have to tweak the knobs of the parameters. Now you need to decide how to build the neural network. This is complex. Who can build a neural network? There are so many degrees of freedom, how do I know what is right? If you're thinking of that. That makes it difficult to use neural network, unless you are in the research team, where you are able to define that. In practice, people don't really build their neural network; usually we base it off some kind of architecture that somebody has created. Deep learning is just a subset of the term. The category of algorithms are just all neural networks, but deep learning just means that we are just building an architecture of a neural network so big and so deep that we just call it deep learning. Then you have your deep neural networks, which are basically the same, but just that we build it, just like your Lego blocks now, your Lego blocks are insanely deep, insanely big. We can also do it for CNN, convolutional neural networks, which we will see on Thursday. We'll talk a bit about recurring neural networks next week. Essentially, the idea here is that neural networks are done in a way where it has a specific bias to the type of data that you are using. You'll start to see that when people create neural networks, there's some kind of intuition which matches with the data. It's super good at handling unstructured data. What this means is that if your data typically is structured, traditional machine learning algorithms still work. It's not saying that just because deep learning now is better, more expressive, it just means that all the algorithms that we learned are useless. These, you can obviously see that it has been dominated using deep learning. In the subsequent lessons, I will give the intuition why it works so well on unstructured data. It's because of this thing called the inductive bias. Because the neural network is like a Lego block that allows you to build all sorts of crazy architectures. You essentially can build an architecture that allows you to capture the bias of the data. Essentially, what is the data's intuition and information that you want to capture, you can actually build it using a neural network. This is just typical illustration. You can basically see that this is just a 3-block neural network, and in the deep learning space, you can have n numbers of blocks. The deeper, the more nonlinear that you introduce, which we will see later on, the deeper the model, the more nonlinear layers you add, the more expressive the model becomes. But then, what happens when the model is very complex and very expressive? Does it mean that I'm saying that the deeper it is, the better? Why is it that the deeper it is, it might not be better? What's the intuition that comes to your mind? Exactly. Your model just becomes so good at just memorizing the data, because the model is just overly complicated. How to define the architecture? It becomes both an art, as well as mostly just following what people have built, from a research standpoint. Unless you are a researcher that builds neural networks, there's no way that you can come up with a neural network that all of a sudden will be the best in the world.
